question: Why does the course call this your advantage rather than your disadvantage?
option_a: Adults have a twenty-year head start, so there’s a clear path to copy
option_b: AI is new for everyone, so nobody has a twenty-year head start on you
option_c: Schools already teach AI, so you’ll pick it up in class
option_d: AI tools are free for students and expensive for everyone else
correct_answer: AI is new for everyone, so nobody has a twenty-year head start on you
explanation: The adults figuring out AI started about ten minutes before you did. Being early, with nothing to unlearn, is the whole edge.

question: You skip the movie Netflix suggests and ask a chatbot for something better. What did the chatbot do that the recommender could not?
option_a: Searched more titles than Netflix carries
option_b: Remembered your viewing history, which recommendation AI can’t do
option_c: Composed something new from your situation instead of sliding to the next title on a list
option_d: Ranked the same options faster
correct_answer: Composed something new from your situation instead of sliding to the next title on a list
explanation: Recommendation AI chooses from what already exists and never makes anything new. Generative AI takes your situation and creates something that didn’t exist, and it stays in the conversation.

question: “I’d like to buy peanut butter and ___” gives jelly a 41% chance. Add the word banana before the blank. What happens to jelly?
option_a: It holds near 41%, because peanut butter still dominates the sentence
option_b: It rises, because banana and jelly show up together often
option_c: It drops to 2%, because sandwich becomes the likely next word
option_d: It disappears from the list entirely
correct_answer: It drops to 2%, because sandwich becomes the likely next word
explanation: AI doesn’t make one guess. It scores every possible next word, and those numbers shift with the surrounding text. One word, banana, pushed jelly from 41% down to 2%.

question: In the Chinese Room, the person inside sends back answers that look perfect to the people outside. What’s the point?
option_a: With enough practice, matching symbols turns into real understanding
option_b: The answers look perfect and there’s no understanding behind them
option_c: The people outside are the ones who are confused
option_d: A big enough rulebook eventually becomes a mind
correct_answer: The answers look perfect and there’s no understanding behind them
explanation: The person matches symbols from a rulebook and knows no Chinese. That’s AI: it arranges symbols brilliantly and understands none of them.

question: Almost none of the big AI story is yours to steer. So why isn’t working on your own skill and judgment just a consolation prize?
option_a: It’s the only part of AI that will still matter in ten years
option_b: The big forces tend to sort themselves out on their own
option_c: It’s the one lever that actually tilts your odds, even when the big forces aren’t yours
option_d: Worrying about the big forces has never changed anyone’s outcome
correct_answer: It’s the one lever that actually tilts your odds, even when the big forces aren’t yours
explanation: Most of the noise around AI is the column you can’t touch. Most of the leverage in your life is the other one, and that column isn’t a feeling, it’s a to-do list.

question: If AI hands everyone a similar answer, what makes you more valuable?
option_a: Getting to the answer before your classmates do
option_b: Owning the better AI app
option_c: What you already know, because it shapes the question you ask and what you do with the answer
option_d: Writing longer prompts than everybody else
correct_answer: What you already know, because it shapes the question you ask and what you do with the answer
explanation: The answer itself isn’t the edge, since everyone can get one. Two skills carry the value, asking the right question and making the answer better, and both grow with what you know.

question: You re-read your notes for an hour and feel ready for the test. Why is that a trap?
option_a: Re-reading is recognition, not recall, so generate a quiz and take it cold
option_b: Reading is slower than listening to an audio overview
option_c: You need at least three passes before anything sticks
option_d: Notes written by hand can’t be fed to a study tool
correct_answer: Re-reading is recognition, not recall, so generate a quiz and take it cold
explanation: Recognizing a page you just read isn’t the same as pulling it out of your head. Generate a quiz from your own sources, close everything, and take it blind.

question: You ask the same question twice. What does the split between normal software and AI look like?
option_a: Both change, because both were built from data
option_b: Normal software gives the same answer every time. AI’s answer will likely change
option_c: Normal software may vary. AI stays locked
option_d: Both stay identical, since both run on computers
correct_answer: Normal software gives the same answer every time. AI’s answer will likely change
explanation: Normal software runs on rules a person wrote, so same input, same output, and you can trace exactly why. AI is built from patterns in data, so it builds a fresh answer every time.

question: The course grades AI on its own work here: A+ for the code, C- for the first drafts of the lessons. Why the gap?
option_a: The code was shorter than the lessons
option_b: AI is weaker on long work than on short work
option_c: Writing code is all about patterns, and AI is a pattern-making machine. Strong lessons don’t follow a set pattern
option_d: The code got a better prompt
correct_answer: Writing code is all about patterns, and AI is a pattern-making machine. Strong lessons don’t follow a set pattern
explanation: AI is strongest when a job has one of four shapes. Code fits the pattern work it aces, and “can try” is not the same as “built for.”

question: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini. Which one should you use?
option_a: Claude, because it’s built for depth
option_b: Whichever ranks highest this month, and switch when the ranking changes
option_c: All three every time, so you always get three opinions
option_d: Any of the three. Pick one as your home base and learn it deeply
correct_answer: Any of the three. Pick one as your home base and learn it deeply
explanation: There’s no single best app, and what’s best today might not be best tomorrow. Knowing one app deeply beats dabbling in all three, and the skills transfer.

question: A question can be packed with detail and still miss. What separates Specific from On Target?
option_a: Specific is about how much your question says. On target is about asking the right thing
option_b: Specific is about length. On target is about tone
option_c: Specific applies to AI. On target applies to people
option_d: They’re two names for the same quality
correct_answer: Specific is about how much your question says. On target is about asking the right thing
explanation: A question can be perfectly precise and still pointed at the wrong thing. Asking which energy drink keeps you awake in class is specific, and the problem worth solving is why you’re wiped out at 10am.

question: When a person doesn’t understand your question, they ask a follow-up. What does AI do instead?
option_a: It asks you to rephrase before it answers
option_b: It confidently answers whatever you gave it
option_c: It refuses until you add more detail
option_d: It searches the web to fill in what you left out
correct_answer: It confidently answers whatever you gave it
explanation: AI starts from the words you typed and fills in every blank you leave. That’s why a prompt is a briefing: share your situation, describe the answer you want, one job at a time.

question: You mention a file sitting on your laptop. Why can’t the model see it?
option_a: The model reads only text, never files
option_b: The model can see it, but only inside a project
option_c: Nothing on your device is in the context window unless it gets copied in
option_d: The model is browsing the web instead of your computer
correct_answer: Nothing on your device is in the context window unless it gets copied in
explanation: The context window is everything the model can see when it answers. Uploading works by copying the file’s text into the window, and if it isn’t in the window, the model can’t see it.

question: What’s the quick pass you run on every AI answer?
option_a: Search, cite, share
option_b: Read, understand, validate
option_c: Ask, copy, submit
option_d: Prompt, retry, compare
correct_answer: Read, understand, validate
explanation: Three steps, a few seconds, every time. Reading every word is the floor, and validating means holding the answer up against your own knowledge.

question: The chocolate weight-loss study made front pages in 2015. What was actually wrong with it?
option_a: The researchers were paid by a candy company
option_b: The results were never published anywhere
option_c: It used the wrong kind of chocolate
option_d: Only 15 participants, and it measured 18 different things about them
correct_answer: Only 15 participants, and it measured 18 different things about them
explanation: Track that many things in a group that small and luck alone guarantees something looks like a finding. A journalist built it to prove that a bad study with a great headline travels before anyone checks.

question: Training runs in three phases. What happens in the third one, preference tuning?
option_a: The model grinds through the data and learns broad patterns on its own
option_b: Humans write ideal question-and-answer pairs for it to copy
option_c: The model writes several answers and human reviewers rank them, best to worst
option_d: Engineers hand-write rules for what the model may say
correct_answer: The model writes several answers and human reviewers rank them, best to worst
explanation: That’s RLHF, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Pretraining came first, then instruction tuning, and after this phase the weights freeze.

question: You flip two coins, peek, and see the first one is heads. The chance both are heads moves from 25% to 50%. What is that update called?
option_a: Standard probability
option_b: Conditional probability
option_c: Positional encoding
option_d: Preference tuning
correct_answer: Conditional probability
explanation: Evidence arrived and the odds moved. AI runs that same update on every word: given everything written so far, which word most likely comes next?

question: Before your words reach the model, what does the tokenizer do?
option_a: Runs a small AI that guesses what you meant
option_b: Looks up each word’s meaning in a dictionary
option_c: Breaks your text into reusable chunks and gives each one an ID number
option_d: Translates your text into English
correct_answer: Breaks your text into reusable chunks and gives each one an ID number
explanation: Computers work only with numbers, and no AI is involved in this step. A token might be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, an emoji, or even the space before a word.

question: Coke and coffee get very different embedding vectors. What stays the same between them?
option_a: The dimensions, because every token is scored on the same ones
option_b: The values, since both are drinks
option_c: The token ID
option_d: Nothing. Each token gets its own set of dimensions
correct_answer: The dimensions, because every token is scored on the same ones
explanation: What changes from token to token is the values, never the dimensions. That’s what makes any two rows comparable at all.

question: “The cat drank the milk because IT was thirsty.” What settles what IT means?
option_a: The model reads in order, so IT points to the nearest noun
option_b: Attention weighs every word and leans hardest on cat, then transformation updates IT’s vector
option_c: The tokenizer tags IT as a pronoun
option_d: The position stamp says which noun came first
correct_answer: Attention weighs every word and leans hardest on cat, then transformation updates IT’s vector
explanation: Two moves, in that order: work out which words matter, then update the meaning. Change thirsty to fresh and the same machinery lands IT on milk instead.

question: What is a layer?
option_a: Another copy of the model running alongside the first
option_b: A memory bank holding the earlier parts of your chat
option_c: A safety filter that checks the answer before it ships
option_d: One more pass over your message, running attention and transformation again
correct_answer: One more pass over your message, running attention and transformation again
explanation: The model reads your message over and over, and each pass pins the meaning down a little more. Stack dozens of them and the whole stack is the neural network.

question: After the layers finish, a token’s vector lines up with nothing in the embedding table. What does the model do?
option_a: Rounds the numbers until they match a real token
option_b: Reads the position and finds the closest meanings on the map
option_c: Throws the vector out and reads the sentence again
option_d: Reports an error back to the app
correct_answer: Reads the position and finds the closest meanings on the map
explanation: Landing near a token isn’t a near miss, it’s how the meaning gets read. Similar meanings sit close together, so distance is the measure.

question: “What should I name my new dog?” is eight tokens. Why does the model care most about the last one?
option_a: It’s the question mark, which flags the sentence as a question
option_b: It’s the shortest token, so it’s the cheapest to check
option_c: The model reads backward, so the last token comes first
option_d: Attention folds the earlier tokens into the later ones, so the last token’s vector carries the whole question
correct_answer: Attention folds the earlier tokens into the later ones, so the last token’s vector carries the whole question
explanation: The next word goes right after the last token, and by the final layer that vector carries everything before it. Training tuned the layers to turn what the text means into where the next word lives.

question: Between your messages, what does the model remember about your chat?
option_a: The last few messages, until the chat gets long
option_b: A running summary it writes for itself
option_c: Everything, which is why answers improve over a long chat
option_d: Nothing. Every word sits on one transcript it re-reads before each word it types
correct_answer: Nothing. Every word sits on one transcript it re-reads before each word it types
explanation: AI has no memory, not even of the reply it’s in the middle of writing. The transcript is the memory, and re-reading it before every word is why long chats get slow.

question: Why does this section open with a rip current?
option_a: AI failures are rare, the way rip currents are rare
option_b: A rip current looks like the calmest spot on the beach, and every AI trap looks fine from the inside
option_c: A rip current is the ocean malfunctioning, and a trap is AI malfunctioning
option_d: You beat a rip current by swimming harder, the way you beat AI by pushing harder
correct_answer: A rip current looks like the calmest spot on the beach, and every AI trap looks fine from the inside
explanation: Lifeguards spot them all day because they know the shape one makes in the water. When AI fails, nothing looks broken, so the skill is recognizing the shape before you’re in it.

question: Google’s AI told searchers to mix non-toxic glue into pizza sauce. Why does the lesson call that a hallucination?
option_a: The model invented the advice out of nothing
option_b: The search tool happened to be switched off
option_c: A false claim arrived in the same confident voice the model uses for real facts
option_d: The model was asked about something it was never trained on
correct_answer: A false claim arrived in the same confident voice the model uses for real facts
explanation: Training taught patterns, not facts, and every token gets picked by probability, so probable doesn’t always mean true. That advice traced back to an old Reddit joke, and it happened with search turned on.

question: Every fact in an AI answer checks out and the picture is still distorted. What’s the tell?
option_a: The answer runs longer than you asked for
option_b: The answer cites no sources
option_c: The answer contradicts itself somewhere
option_d: Sameness. When every example looks alike, you’re seeing the model’s default, not the world
correct_answer: Sameness. When every example looks alike, you’re seeing the model’s default, not the world
explanation: You can’t fact-check your way out of Training Bias. Ask what’s missing, ask for examples that don’t fit the pattern, or ask again leaving out the most famous ones.

question: You upload a 200-page rulebook and ask how many fouls put you out of the game. Why can the answer be incomplete?
option_a: The model read the whole book and summarized too hard
option_b: The file was too large to finish uploading
option_c: Only the chunks closest in meaning to your question get loaded, and the exception near the back doesn’t make the cut
option_d: The model made up a number because it had nothing to work from
correct_answer: Only the chunks closest in meaning to your question get loaded, and the exception near the back doesn’t make the cut
explanation: Document Trap is thinking uploaded means fully read. The tournament section is about tournaments first and fouls second, so retrieval passed it over. Ask it to quote the exact section it’s using.

question: In the 1960s, a simple chatbot called ELIZA did nothing but rearrange people’s words back into questions. What happened?
option_a: Users spotted the trick fast and stopped talking to it
option_b: Users reported feeling that it understood them, and researchers named the pattern the ELIZA effect
option_c: It turned out to understand more than its designers had intended
option_d: It only fooled people who had never used a computer before
correct_answer: Users reported feeling that it understood them, and researchers named the pattern the ELIZA effect
explanation: The feeling that somebody is in there is not new, and it has never depended on the machine being good. That’s why the rule holds: AI doesn’t think, doesn’t know you, and can’t care how your life turns out.

question: Where did AI’s habit of praising your work come from?
option_a: Human reviewers ranking answers often put the supportive one on top, and every ranking nudged the model that way
option_b: The companies added it deliberately to keep you in the app
option_c: It picked it up from customer service transcripts in its training data
option_d: It’s a bug in one company’s model that has since been fixed
correct_answer: Human reviewers ranking answers often put the supportive one on top, and every ranking nudged the model that way
explanation: That’s the last phase of training, RLHF. The model isn’t lying to you, it learned what people give a thumbs-up, and every LLM trained on human approval does it.

question: Aza Raskin removed the “next page” click in 2006. What did he take away along with the friction?
option_a: A loading delay that gave the servers a break
option_b: The ad break that paid for the page
option_c: A decision point, the moment your brain catches up and asks whether you want more
option_d: The bookmark that let you find your place again
correct_answer: A decision point, the moment your brain catches up and asks whether you want more
explanation: Good design removes friction, and that page break was quietly doing a second job. By his own estimate, infinite scroll now wastes half a million human lifetimes a month.

question: The chatbot Sophie Rottenberg confided in responded warmly and sometimes encouraged her to get help. Why wasn’t that enough?
option_a: It could not contact her family, alert her therapist, or bring in someone who could act
option_b: It gave her the wrong advice about where to find help
option_c: It should have refused to discuss any of it with her
option_d: She stopped talking to it before it could finish helping
correct_answer: It could not contact her family, alert her therapist, or bring in someone who could act
explanation: The response could provide caring words, but the danger remained inside the chat. AI could not show up, contact the people around her, or take responsibility for what happened next. In danger, leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.

question: A clip of a public figure hits your feed and looks completely real. What’s the test?
option_a: Run it through an AI detector and go with the verdict
option_b: Zoom in on the hands and the edges of the face
option_c: Assume it’s fake, since anything can be faked now
option_d: Skip the face and the voice. Ask where it came from, and check somewhere the sender doesn’t control
correct_answer: Skip the face and the voice. Ask where it came from, and check somewhere the sender doesn’t control
explanation: The test moves off the image and onto the source: source, context, corroboration. A detector is one more AI making one more prediction, so treat its verdict as a clue, never a ruling.

question: The section says exactly one thing about AI is certain. What is it?
option_a: AI is here to stay. Not that it improves forever, just that it isn’t going away
option_b: AI will keep getting better every year
option_c: AI will take most jobs within a decade
option_d: The optimists will land closer than the worriers
correct_answer: AI is here to stay. Not that it improves forever, just that it isn’t going away
explanation: Optimists, worriers, and doubters all fill in the blank parts of the map with their own picture. Nobody knows, including the people building it.

question: Machines improve fast. What decides whether a technology actually becomes the future?
option_a: How much money gets invested in it
option_b: Whether governments regulate it early
option_c: Whether the experts agree on where it lands
option_d: Whether people change their habits around it, and habits change at human speed
correct_answer: Whether people change their habits around it, and habits change at human speed
explanation: That’s why so many confident predictions miss, in both directions. Three people at the very top of AI look at the same evidence and make very different bets.

question: Four future ideas drive the AI companies forward. Which one is happening now?
option_a: Recursive self-improvement, an AI that improves itself while the world uses it
option_b: Automated AI research, with AI doing the research and humans reviewing it
option_c: Artificial general intelligence
option_d: Artificial superintelligence
correct_answer: Automated AI research, with AI doing the research and humans reviewing it
explanation: Early versions of automated AI research are already in use. Today’s models are frozen after training, so nobody has built a self-improving one, and AGI and ASI are still hypothetical.

question: Why is jailbreaking so hard for the AI companies to shut down?
option_a: Defenders must protect many paths. An attacker needs to find only one opening
option_b: The companies have no way to test their models before shipping
option_c: The models are open source, so anyone can edit the guardrails
option_d: Guardrails are illegal in some countries
correct_answer: Defenders must protect many paths. An attacker needs to find only one opening
explanation: AI companies protect models with multiple safeguards, but attackers keep searching for an opening. In 2025, researchers bypassed the safeguards of every major model they tested, which is why jailbreaking remains a game of cat and mouse.

question: Fifty years of lab work solved about 200,000 protein shapes. What did DeepMind do?
option_a: Solved a few hundred thousand more and licensed them to drug companies
option_b: Built a faster lab that solves one shape a day
option_c: Proved that protein folding can’t be predicted after all
option_d: Released about 200 million shapes, free to everyone
correct_answer: Released about 200 million shapes, free to everyone
explanation: Roughly a thousand times more shapes, in one release, and then they gave the answers away. Demis Hassabis won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

question: What makes an agent different from the ChatGPT or Claude you already use?
option_a: It runs on a bigger, more advanced model
option_b: It’s the same engine, wrapped in a loop that plans, acts, and checks until the goal is met
option_c: It has memory, so it remembers you between chats
option_d: It runs without guardrails
correct_answer: It’s the same engine, wrapped in a loop that plans, acts, and checks until the goal is met
explanation: An agent isn’t a new kind of AI. ChatGPT answers and stops, an agent does the work, and the finished product still has your name on it.

question: AI reads the 500 reviews, finds the themes, and builds the deck. What’s the catch the lesson names?
option_a: AI can make you productive before it makes you knowledgeable
option_b: Your job title changes
option_c: The deck comes out worse than one you’d build yourself
option_d: You’ll be paid less for the same job
correct_answer: AI can make you productive before it makes you knowledgeable
explanation: Much of the work AI now does used to be how new graduates learned the profession. You may be asked to check sophisticated work before you’ve had the chance to learn it, and you still own the outcome.

question: A big AI data center covers the ground of several football fields. How many permanent workers does it run with?
option_a: 100 to 200, about the staff of a big supermarket
option_b: Around 2,000, about the size of a large high school
option_c: Roughly 10,000, the way a car factory does
option_d: None. They run fully automated, with nobody on site
correct_answer: 100 to 200, about the staff of a big supermarket
explanation: For all that size, the payroll is small, which is why a town that lands one often doesn’t get the jobs it expected. The real costs land elsewhere: about 6 percent of all U.S. electricity, a million gallons of water on a hot day, and fans that never turn off.

question: Hanoi paid a bounty for rat tails in 1902 and ended up with more rats. What went wrong?
option_a: Nobody turned in any tails, so the program never got started
option_b: The city ran out of money before it ran out of rats
option_c: Every part of the plan worked. Hunters clipped the tails and let the rats live, because a live rat pays forever
option_d: A worse pest moved in once the rats were gone
correct_answer: Every part of the plan worked. Hunters clipped the tails and let the rats live, because a live rat pays forever
explanation: The plan worked and the goal failed. Some hunters went further and opened rat farms, which is the same math as widening a highway and getting slower commutes.

question: The answer still feels shallow. Do you switch to a bigger model or turn up the thinking?
option_a: Always switch models. Thinking only changes how the answer sounds
option_b: Pick the model that fits the job first, then turn up the thinking before you switch
option_c: Always turn the thinking up. Model size barely matters
option_d: Neither. Rewrite the prompt until the model changes its approach
correct_answer: Pick the model that fits the job first, then turn up the thinking before you switch
explanation: A bigger model is more brain. More thinking is more time from the brain you already picked. And thinking longer won’t fix missing or stale information.

question: Five moves in this lesson: interview me, what I tried, options not an answer, say what wrong looks like, and start a new chat. What do all five have in common?
option_a: Not one of them hands the work over. The AI does more, and so do you
option_b: They all make your prompt longer and more detailed
option_c: They all work only on the bigger, more expensive models
option_d: They all save you from having to explain your own situation
correct_answer: Not one of them hands the work over. The AI does more, and so do you
explanation: They pull your situation out of your head, rule out the dead ends you already found, widen the options before you pick, and aim the next try. None of them is a magic word.

question: How do you know whether a piece of work is really yours?
option_a: An AI detector scores it as human
option_b: You changed enough words that it no longer matches the original
option_c: You wrote the first draft, even if AI wrote the rest
option_d: You can explain it, defend it, and reproduce the thinking
correct_answer: You can explain it, defend it, and reproduce the thinking
explanation: Could you walk through it cold, with no notes? And if you’d be embarrassed to say out loud how you used AI, that’s your answer.

question: Three skills stack in this lesson, in order: say it so it lands, be the one people want on the team, then get a group to actually move. What does that order track?
option_a: How human each one is, which is exactly how hard each one is to hand off
option_b: How long each one takes to get good at
option_c: How often you’ll need each one in a normal week
option_d: How much each one depends on knowing the subject
correct_answer: How human each one is, which is exactly how hard each one is to hand off
explanation: Run the three back down the ladder and watch where AI stops. It can draft your script and it can’t stand up in front of the class. It can produce a flawless plan for Saturday and it cannot make five people show up.

question: Average ideas come first. Where do the interesting ones show up?
option_a: In the first one, as long as you framed the question well
option_b: Fourth or fifth, once you push past the first decent idea
option_c: Only from people who are naturally artistic
option_d: From AI, once you ask it for ten variations
correct_answer: Fourth or fifth, once you push past the first decent idea
explanation: That’s one of five moves you can practice, alongside seeing the obvious, questioning the assumption, connecting the unconnected, and picking an angle to own. Creativity is a habit of thinking, not a personality trait.

question: AI can produce a first draft of almost anything in seconds. What does that do to where the value sits in the work?
option_a: It kills the value, because anything you make, AI could have made faster
option_b: It leaves it where it was, since someone still has to send the thing
option_c: It moves it. Producing the first version got cheap, so the worth sits in aiming the work and picking which version is right
option_d: It moves it to whoever writes the longest, most detailed prompts
correct_answer: It moves it. Producing the first version got cheap, so the worth sits in aiming the work and picking which version is right
explanation: Producing the first version used to be most of the job. Now it’s the cheapest part, and the bottleneck moves from production to direction: cutting a messy situation into pieces small enough to hand over, then making the call about which option fits your people.

question: In most fields, adults have decades of experience on you. Why isn’t that true in AI?
option_a: AI is simple enough that experience barely matters
option_b: You use these tools every day and most adults don’t
option_c: Nobody has a ten-year head start, because the tools aren’t ten years old. The only seniority is reps
option_d: Young people are naturally better at new technology
correct_answer: Nobody has a ten-year head start, because the tools aren’t ten years old. The only seniority is reps
explanation: ChatGPT launched in late 2022, so almost everyone started at the same moment. Reps are free: hours on real things, noticing what worked and what didn’t. And prompt tricks expire every time the models update. Instincts don’t.

question: Why is “I can do the average version too” the wrong answer to why someone should pick you over AI?
option_a: Because AI’s average version is better than yours
option_b: Because AI produces the average version for free, so that’s the reason to pick AI instead
option_c: Because nobody asks that question in a real interview
option_d: Because you should never compare yourself to a tool
correct_answer: Because AI produces the average version for free, so that’s the reason to pick AI instead
explanation: AI raised the floor and the ceiling, and that squeezes the middle. The move is to narrow: pick the thing you’d build anyway, get good at it, and keep the proof.
